transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, what brings me in is... I keep getting hit out of nowhere with this scene of my cousin on that pavement. It's so real, like I can hear the shouting and see the lights all over again. And it just happens suddenly, even when I'm just standing in the church office trying to do my job and act normal. It's getting really hard to deal with.

When you have these sudden memories of your cousin, do you feel like you're actually back there experiencing it again in that moment, or does it feel more like you're watching a memory from a distance?

It feels like I'm actually back there. I mean, it's not like I'm just remembering it, it's... I can smell the exhaust, I can feel the cold ground. It's like I'm right back on that street. I completely lose track of where I actually am for a minute.

latest_inference.note: Patient describes intrusive flashbacks with full sensory immersion (smell, touch, visual, auditory), dissociation from present environment, and sudden triggering - classic for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). The vivid re-experiencing with loss of awareness of current location is pathognomonic for PTSD flashbacks. F43.12 (acute stress disorder) is less likely given the apparent duration suggests chronic presentation. F41.1 (generalized anxiety) and F48.1 (other anxiety disorders) do not explain the dissociative flashback phenomenology.
